<reason>Both sides were excellent, but B built the more durable path. A's best move was the trap: CON cannot call the numbers both worthless and costly. B dissolved it squarely with the noise-to-the-price-taker / leash-on-the-price-setter asymmetry, explaining how a band can fail to inform workers yet still tax managers, with workers paying via compression and vanished slow-build roles. A's closing reasserted the trap ("if managers feel a leash, workers have seen a price") without answering the asymmetry; B's reply that the leash constrains without informing landed cleanly. B also sustained the stronger compression mechanism (public justification costs, not locked steps), converted A's concessions into a cumulative "blurry, captioned, gamed, redacted" signal, and supplied the cleaner decision rule of net benefit. A scored real points (outside offers price exit, not the job; roll-ups answer small cells) and matched B rhetorically, keeping this competitive rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 / closing exchange dissolving A's "worthless vs. expensive" contradiction: the same band is noise to the worker reading it and a leash on the manager writing it because they are different people — "That asymmetry is not a contradiction in our case. It is the case."</best_rebuttal>
